title: Few, little, less, fewer
subtitle: what little money / fewer than 20 students
summary: Use (a) few and (a) little precisely, including the few / what little, and choose between less (than) and fewer (than).

lesson.heading: (a) few and (a) little as pronouns
lesson.text: As well as standing in front of nouns, (a) few and (a) little can be used on their own as pronouns when it is clear what we are talking about.

examples.text: It is a part of the world visited by **few**.
Do you want a chocolate? There's still **a few** left.
**Little** is known about the painter's early life.
*A:* Do you know anything about car engines? *B:* **A little**.
examples.note: = I know a little about car engines

lesson.note: quite a few means 'quite a large number': She's been away from work for quite a few weeks.

lesson.heading: the few / the little and what few / what little
lesson.text: the few + noun suggests there are not enough things or people, and the little + noun that we only have part of the amount we need. what few / what little means 'the small number' or 'the small amount' - all there was.

examples.text: It's one of **the few** shops in the city centre where you can buy food.
We should use **the little** time we have available to discuss Jon's proposal.
She gave **what little** money she had in her purse to the man.
**What few** visitors we have are always made welcome.

lesson.note: When the context makes it clear, the noun can be dropped: She gave what / the little she had ...; What / The few we have ...

lesson.heading: few after my, her, these, those
lesson.text: few (but rarely little) can follow a possessive such as my or her, and these or those.

examples.text: I learned to play golf during my **few** days off during the summer.
These **few** miles of motorway have taken over ten years to build.

left.label: Speech and informal writing
left.text: We prefer not many / much, only / just ... a few / little, and a bit (of) instead of a little.
examples: Sorry I haven't finished, I **haven't had much** time today.
I won't be long. I've **only got a few** things to get.

right.label: Formal and academic writing
right.text: Here few and little are the natural choice.
examples: The results take **little** account of personal preference.
The country **has had few** female politicians since independence.
There **seems to be little** prospect of ever recovering the missing manuscript.

lesson.heading: less or fewer?
lesson.text: less goes with uncountable nouns and fewer with plural countable nouns. less + plural countable noun is common in conversation but grammatically incorrect.

examples.text: There are **fewer** cars on the road today.

lesson.heading: less than or fewer than?
lesson.text: less than goes with a noun phrase indicating an amount, and fewer than with a noun phrase referring to a group of things or people. Distances and sums of money always take less than.

examples.text: I used to earn **less than** a pound a week when I first started work.
There were **fewer than** 20 students at the lecture.
examples.note: informally ... less than ..., though some people think that is incorrect

examples.text: The beach is **less than** a mile away.

lesson.heading: no less than / no fewer than
lesson.text: To stress that a number is surprisingly large we use no less than or no fewer than. With percentages, periods of time and quantities we prefer no less than.

examples.text: The team has had **no fewer than** ten managers in just five years.
Profits have increased by **no less than** 95% in the last year.

lesson.text: Test yourself with 'how many?' or 'how much?': how many takes few / fewer, how much takes little / less.

exercises.prompt: ___ remains of the old castle walls except the Black Gate.
exercises.explanation: little used as a pronoun here means 'not much'.
a little as a pronoun means 'a small amount' - a positive answer.

exercises.prompt: Thomas was named sportsperson of the year, and ___ would disagree.
exercises.explanation: few = few people. a few would mean that a small number of people actually do disagree.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Have there been many applications for the job? *B:* Yes, quite ___.
exercises.explanation: quite a few means 'quite a large number'.

exercises.prompt: ___ belongings she had were packed into a small suitcase.
exercises.explanation: the few / what few + plural noun means 'the small number she had' - not many.

exercises.prompt: I don't have much money, but I'm happy to lend you ___ I have.
exercises.explanation: With no noun after it we can still say the little or what little to mean 'the small amount'.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Did you do anything last night? *B:* I just watched ___ and then went to bed.
exercises.explanation: In this informal, spoken context a bit of is more natural than a little.

exercises.prompt: In an academic history of the country: The country ___ female politicians since independence.
exercises.explanation: In formal, academic writing few is preferred to not many.

exercises.statement: There are less cars on the road today.
exercises.explanation: There are fewer cars on the road today. less with a plural countable noun is heard in conversation but is grammatically incorrect.

exercises.prompt: Does the gap need less or fewer?

items.text: There are ___ cars on the road today.
I used to earn ___ than a pound a week.
There were ___ than 20 students at the lecture.
The beach is ___ than a mile away.
Male students spend ___ money than female students on books.

exercises.prompt: Profits have increased by no ___ 95% in the last year.
exercises.explanation: With percentages, periods of time and quantities we prefer no less than.

exercises.prompt: Comment on the survey: in 2000 more students had a part-time job than they do now.
exercises.answer: Fewer students had a part-time job in 2000 than now.
exercises.explanation: students is a plural countable noun, so fewer.
